scopeReview: IMP-5.B.1–4: contextual biotechnology/aquaculture evaluation, food-choice movements and direct sales, food access/distribution/weather and suburban land conversion, and policy/economic incentives. No universal GMO, organic, local-food or fair-trade benefit/harm claim.
varietyReview: Four meaningful stimuli:target-pest yield comparison, original store-travel map, direct-sale terms and aquaculture input/discharge accounts. Checks compare response differences, unique travel maximum, advance cash/risk terms and feed ratios. Applied cases cover labels, urban growing, premiums, diets and policy.
repetitionReview: Access, contextual trait performance, contract timing and feed conversion are distinct tasks. The final affordability case distinguishes price constraints from geographic travel; no exact repeated stem or numerical-only clone. Original synthetic evidence, detailed options and varied keys; difficulty uncalibrated.
referenceNote: Primary aquaculture research themes and USDA CSA risk-sharing description checked. No actual cultivar, medical claim, current legal certification rule, third-party content or resource imported. Fictional sale terms are not legal advice; no independent human review claimed.

questions.correctOption: The observed yield benefit depends on the target pest’s pressure; the trial does not establish every environmental or economic outcome.
questions.independentReview: Independently compared matched yields5−3=2 under pressure and5−5=0 without. Trait specifically targets one insect, not all pests or drought. No health/safety inference, chemical-use quantity or universal GMO effect claimed.

questions.correctOption: Central, with a 50-minute one-way trip; access still requires evidence beyond a travel-time map.
questions.independentReview: Checked the maximum50 is unique and means one-way median travel, not distance, income or all-household behavior. Avoided assigning a formal real-world food-desert designation from one metric alone.

questions.correctOption: Arrangement A, because members prepay for a harvest share rather than a guaranteed quantity.
questions.independentReview: Checked contract terms as a hypothetical CSA example, not a claim all CSAs use identical rules. No legal contract interpretation or guaranteed farmer profit asserted; members’ cash timing and risk terms are separate.

questions.correctOption: B uses less feed per tonne and releases less of the measured nutrient, but other impacts still need assessment.
questions.independentReview: Independently recomputed feed ratios2.0/1.2 and nutrient reduction60%. No assumption all fish species/systems share those efficiencies or that feed ingredients have identical upstream effects.

questions.correctOption: Measures of relevant outcomes and inputs under comparable conditions, rather than assume one label proves every outcome.
questions.independentReview: Avoided unverified current certification rules or universal health claims. Question asks evidence for a broad impact claim, not whether any particular label is legally valid.

questions.correctOption: It could add a nearby food source, but land suitability, water, tenure, costs and distribution still affect feasibility and access.
questions.independentReview: A hypothetical planning assessment, not practical soil-treatment advice or an actual health/safety claim. No automatic food-security guarantee from geographic proximity.

questions.correctOption: Growers’ actual net returns and payment terms, including added costs and how the premium is distributed.
questions.independentReview: No current certification guarantee, named fair-trade organization or actual premium claimed. Distinguishes final product price from producer outcomes and allows possible benefits without asserting universality.

questions.correctOption: Housing needs, lost production capacity, infrastructure and environmental effects should be examined together.
questions.independentReview: Aligned farmland loss to suburbanization in IMP-5.B.3 without prescribing a real zoning decision or assuming uniform soil value, food supply or housing demand.

questions.correctOption: Greater demand for feed crops and associated land, water or input use along the production chain.
questions.independentReview: Used a stated hypothetical input difference rather than an unsupported livestock/crop footprint statistic. No dietary health guidance or claim that all animal foods use identical feed systems.

questions.correctOption: The policy changes an incentive, but suitability, operating costs, knowledge and access can still produce uneven uptake.
questions.independentReview: Hypothetical incentive, not a current subsidy or legal entitlement. Conditional uptake reasoning avoids guaranteeing profitability or requiring a farmer to adopt.

questions.correctOption: Physical availability and affordable access are different dimensions; increasing supply alone may not resolve the stated barrier.
questions.independentReview: Separated an explicitly stated affordability constraint from transport access in the map item. No specific real food-insecurity threshold or program recommendation introduced.
